Krynki Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Krynki, Poland

Not demolished. Krynki, recorded as a prince's village by the mid-15th century and granted town rights by Sigismund II Augustus in 1569, saw Jewish settlement from the 16th century; a 1662 royal permission to build a synagogue and cemetery was confirmed in 1745, and the community gained independence from Grodno's kehilla in 1691. Before Poland's partitions, Krynki held one of the country's largest Jewish communities; under Russian rule it developed into a significant industrial center with Jewish involvement, peaking around 5,000 residents (75%) by 1914, still 60% (about 4,000) by 1939. Germans established a ghetto in fall 1941, liquidated in stages through fall 1942 to Treblinka; the ghetto's last Jews were shot on Passover 1943. This cemetery, likely established in the 17th century and expanded repeatedly through the interwar period, holds postwar reburials of exhumed local Holocaust victims alongside its historic graves.
